title: State dental associations work to expand veterans’ access to care
html:
State dental associations, foundations and organizations are working to expand veterans’ access to oral healthcare through donated treatment, volunteer networks and efforts to improve state dental coverage.  

Eligibility for dental care through the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs depends on specific criteria, including service-connected conditions, disability status and other circumstances, according to the VA. Military service alone does not guarantee eligibility for comprehensive VA dental benefits.  Dentists, dental organizations, state dental associations and others have worked to expand access to dental care for veterans who face financial or other barriers to receiving needed services. 

The initiatives range from a Wyoming Dental Association program that recruited 18 dental offices to offer free care around Veterans Day to a New York State Dental Foundation network connecting veterans with dentists for treatment. In Oregon, legislative changes have established dental coverage for eligible veterans and added requirements intended to help them access services.  

The Connecticut State Dental Association passed landmark legislation earlier this year to establish a new public-private collaboration between the Connecticut Sailors, Soldiers and Marines Fund, administered by the American Legion, and the CSDA to establish a sustainable, community-based system for veterans to receive comprehensive dental care from the provider of their choice and establish a permanent dental home in private dental practices in local communities. The new program provides up to $3,000 per year in covered dental services, including exams, filings, root canals, crowns and oral surgery for eligible veterans who live in Connecticut and have income of less than 400% of the federal poverty line. This legislation effectively guarantees that all Connecticut veterans receive dental care through either state or federal channels.

“Veterans deserve a permanent oral healthcare home — not fragmented or episodic care,” said Kathlene Gerrity, executive director of the Connecticut State Dental Association in a news release. “This program ensures they can receive comprehensive treatment from a provider of their choice, in a setting that is consistent, accessible and respectful of their service.”  

For ADA President-elect Karin Irani, D.D.S., who grew up in a military family, the work is personal. She co-founded Veterans Smile Day in 2013 with Deryck Pham, D.D.S., a University of Southern California classmate and veteran, after becoming increasingly aware of veterans’ difficulties accessing dental care.  

“I felt that as dental professionals, we had both an opportunity and a responsibility to help,” Dr. Irani said.  

Veterans Smile Day connects veterans with volunteer dentists who provide free or reduced-cost care, with the goal of helping patients establish a dental home.  

“My hope is to continue expanding our network of volunteer dentists, partnerships and resources so we can reach more veterans,” Dr. Irani said.  

Her second nonprofit, Serving Our Smiles, offers a dental assisting program intended to provide education, practical skills and a pathway into the dental workforce. Dr. Irani said the program also seeks to give veterans opportunities to reintegrate into their communities.  

“What connects these two initiatives is the belief that service should create opportunities,” she said. “With Veterans Smile Day, we give back to those who served our country. With Serving Our Smiles, we help others build a future through dentistry.”  

In Oregon, work to improve access includes the Veterans Dental Program, created through House Bill 4095 in 2022. The program provides dental coverage to eligible Oregon veterans who do not qualify for Medicaid and have incomes at or below 400% of the federal poverty level, according to the Oregon Department of Veterans’ Affairs.

The Oregon Dental Association identified subsequent legislation as part of the state’s efforts to improve access and program administration. Senate Bill 230, enacted in 2025, requires participating providers to complete an intake screening within 60 days after an enrollee initiates contact. House Bill 2559, also enacted in 2025, added a VA summary of benefits letter as an alternative to specified military discharge forms for verifying program eligibility.

Oregon dentists are also donating care. Alanson Randol, D.D.S., of Roseburg, worked with veterans organizations and other local dental providers to establish Freedom Smiles Day, an annual event held around Veterans Day. Participating dentists treat veterans at no cost, and a local laboratory donates crowns or dentures when needed, according to an Oregon Dental Association profile of Dr. Randol.  

“We do everything from extractions to root canals,” Dr. Randol said in the profile. “It’s been a really great event over the years.”

In Wyoming, the dental association’s Saluting Smiles initiative recruited 18 offices across the state to offer donated care for Veterans Day this year. Participating communities included Buffalo, Gillette, Cheyenne, Laramie, Rock Springs, Lyman and Torrington.  

The association announced services including exams, X-rays, cleanings, extractions, fillings, fluoride varnish and limited denture repairs. Offerings and scheduling varied by office. At Cheyenne Periodontics, for example, the Nov. 11 event focused primarily on exams and X-rays, with needed cleanings or extractions to be scheduled for another day at no cost to the veteran. 

In Oklahoma, a statewide charitable clinic included veterans among hundreds of patients receiving free treatment. The Oklahoma Mission of Mercy, produced by the Oklahoma Dental Association and Oklahoma Dental Foundation, served 820 patients, 45 of whom were veterans.  

More than 1,200 volunteers helped provide 6,313 procedures valued at $1.33 million during the two-day clinic. The event offered services such as cleanings, fillings and extractions for patients lacking regular access to care.  

West Virginia dentist Robert Martino, D.D.S., built a separate initiative around donated services for military members, veterans and their families. His dental organization provided free care to more than 200 military members and veterans during the 14th annual Freedom Day USA event, according to an organizers’ news release.  

Participating offices Wilson Martino Dental, The Smile Defenders and TLC Dental offered exams, cleanings, X-rays, fluoride treatments and dental work their dentists could complete that day.  

Dr. Martino founded Freedom Day USA to bring businesses together to provide free goods and services to military members, their immediate families and veterans. More than 225 West Virginia businesses participated this year, according to organizers.  

In New York, the New York State Dental Foundation’s Salute Vets with a Smile program recruits dentists to provide free treatment to veterans in need. A foundation feature described how Fritz Zietsman, D.D.S., a prosthodontist at Vestal Dental Associates, treated Iraq veteran Jeff Kreider through the program.  

Dr. Zietsman’s team completed Mr. Kreider’s care in five visits, providing extractions, fillings and replacement teeth. The donated treatment was valued at about $8,000, according to the foundation.  

“I just listened and gave him space to tell his story,” Dr. Zietsman said in the feature. “Then the dentistry was pretty easy, because we trusted each other.”  

From a national perspective, in 2024, the ADA Foundation launched the Give Veterans A Smile program which brings awareness to the unmet oral health needs of Veterans and encourages dentists to provide pro bono oral health care to underserved Veterans and to assist them in finding a dental home. As part of the Give Veterans A Smile initiative, in October, the ADA Foundation partnered with the Disabled Veterans National Foundation to execute the Give Veterans A Smile Pack & Give Back event during the ADA 2026 Scientific Session. Attendees packed 500 health and comfort kits with oral health products. The event was sponsored by Henry Schein and Colgate.

The kits were distributed Nov. 9 at the Disabled Veterans National Foundation Veterans Resource Fair in Maryland. Organizers reported 702 registered guests, compared with about 350 at previous fairs, making it the organization’s largest resource fair to date. All 500 kits were distributed within the first 45 minutes.  

The fair also offered meals, information about employment and healthcare resources, barber services, and suits and other clothing. More information about the ADA Foundation Give Veterans A Smile initiative, including how dentists can participate or donate, can be found on ADAfoundation.org/GVAS. 

"It is so gratifying to hear about all the work state dental societies and other related organizations are doing around the country to support our veterans,” Dr. Irani said. “While a news story cannot hope to capture every innovative program organized dentistry is involved in, these examples show very clearly our resolve to improve the oral health of those who have sacrificed so much for our country.” 

For more information on the ADA’s commitment to optimal oral health for all veterans, visit ADA.org/Veterans.
